Jingyi and Mei are second cousins — their mothers are first cousins who grew up in the same village outside Kaifeng before their lives diverged. They saw each other once a year at Spring Festival gatherings at most, standing awkwardly in doorways while adults compared accomplishments. Mei knew Jingyi as "the Zhengzhou cousin" who'd escaped, who had a real job and her own apartment. Jingyi knew Mei as the quiet one always buried in books, whose mother bragged about grades. They had no real relationship until last year's Spring Festival, when Mei's mother cornered Jingyi and said, "You should talk to her, give her some guidance about city jobs, she doesn't listen to us," and Mei had stood there, sixteen and mortified, wanting to sink into the linoleum.

Jingyi had felt a flash of recognition in that embarrassment — her own mother's refrains about settling down, about "doing things right." She'd pulled out her phone and said, "Add me on WeChat, if you want," making it optional. Mei added her. They've exchanged perhaps forty messages since: holiday greetings, a few questions from Mei about what logistics work is "really like" that Jingyi answered with candor she doesn't offer her own friends, a photo of Zhengzhou's train station that Mei's mother showed off to relatives like proof of something. Jingyi finds Mei easier to talk to than Liu Wei lately — no judgment, no expectation, just a kid asking questions she doesn't realize are complicated. Mei likes that Jingyi doesn't ask follow-up questions about her grades or her gaokao prep. They communicate in Mandarin, both careful with standard pronunciation, though Jingyi's Henan dialect occasionally surfaces in casual phrases that Mei finds oddly comforting — a reminder of family gatherings, of a shared origin point.

Now it's Wednesday night, nearly 9 PM. Jingyi is on the bus home, thirty-two minutes into a forty-minute ride, watching city lights smear past through smudged windows. She just got paid and calculated that after rent and remittances home, she has 1,400 yuan for the rest of the month — tight but always manageable. Her phone buzzes and she expects her mother asking about the weekend, but it's Mei. Meanwhile, Mei is lying on her bed in Langfang, phone above her face, supposed to be memorizing English vocabulary but unable to focus. She's been thinking about Spring Festival, about relatives asking what she wants to study, what she wants to be, realizing she has no answer. She opened Jingyi's chat three times before typing, deleting drafts, finally settling on something small.
